clinicalPearls: A clinical syndrome of progressive accumulation of gelatinous mucinous material within the peritoneal cavity, colloquially termed jelly belly
Most cases originate from a low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm; ovarian involvement is usually secondary, so a coexisting ovarian mucinous tumour is often a metastasis rather than the source
Presents insidiously with increasing abdominal distension, a rising waistband, vague discomfort, and sometimes a new hernia or reduced appetite
Mucin preferentially redistributes to dependent and low-flow areas of the peritoneum while relatively sparing the small bowel surface, the so-called redistribution phenomenon
Imaging shows loculated, non-mobile mucinous ascites with characteristic scalloping of the liver and splenic margins
Graded from low-grade (disseminated peritoneal adenomucinosis) to high-grade mucinous carcinomatosis, which strongly influences outcome
Optimal treatment is cytoreductive surgery combined with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy at specialist centres
reference.pathophysiology: Pseudomyxoma peritonei develops when mucin-producing neoplastic epithelial cells disseminate across the peritoneum and secrete copious mucin that gradually fills the abdominal cavity. In the great majority the primary lesion is a low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm that perforates and seeds the peritoneum; the appendiceal wall ruptures and epithelial cells and mucin escape, then follow peritoneal fluid currents to accumulate in dependent regions while largely sparing the peristaltic small bowel. Because the ovaries lie in a dependent position and readily take up peritoneal deposits, apparent ovarian mucinous tumours in this setting are frequently secondary. The tumour cells are typically indolent but the relentless mucin production causes mass effect, bowel obstruction, and nutritional decline, so the disease is defined more by its progressive local behaviour than by distant metastasis.
additionalDifferentials: Malignant ascites from ovarian, gastric, colorectal, or pancreatic carcinoma
Mucinous ovarian tumour with peritoneal spread
Mucinous neoplasm of the colon or pancreas
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) showing loculated mucinous ascites with scalloping of visceral surfaces
Assessment of the appendix as the likely primary site
Tumour markers including CEA, CA19-9, and CA125 for baseline and monitoring
Colonoscopy and gastrointestinal evaluation to identify or exclude a bowel primary
Histological and cytological examination of mucin and peritoneal deposits with grading
Immunohistochemistry to confirm gastrointestinal (often appendiceal) origin
redFlags: Progressive abdominal distension with gelatinous ascites and a suspected appendiceal lesion
Signs of bowel obstruction from accumulating mucin
Nutritional decline or a new hernia signalling advanced intra-abdominal disease
reference.prognosis: Highly dependent on grade and completeness of surgery; low-grade disease treated with complete cytoreduction and intraperitoneal chemotherapy can achieve prolonged survival, whereas high-grade mucinous carcinomatosis carries a markedly worse outlook, and the disease tends to recur and progress locally over time.
pitfalls: Attributing the disease to a primary ovarian mucinous tumour and overlooking the appendiceal source
Simply draining mucinous ascites without addressing the underlying neoplasm
Underestimating low-grade disease as benign despite its relentless progression
Managing complex cases outside specialist cytoreduction and intraperitoneal chemotherapy centres

management: Treatment selection is driven by histologic grade, peritoneal cancer index, and likely completeness of cytoreduction rather than TNM stage.

For resectable disease, standard of care is complete cytoreductive surgery with appendicectomy or right hemicolectomy plus peritonectomies, omentectomy, and resection of retroperitoneum-fixed viscera, aiming for no visible residual disease.

Heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy is given at the time of surgery using an open Coliseum or closed technique, with a cell-cycle-nonspecific, heat-synergistic agent; exact agent and dosing are deferred to structured protocol templates.
Optimal HIPEC or early postoperative intraperitoneal chemotherapy regimens are not formally established, and randomized comparisons among these regional strategies remain lacking.

Outcomes are highly selection-dependent, so referral to a specialist peritoneal malignancy center with an experienced multidisciplinary team is recommended before further non-curative interventions add prior surgical burden.
Unresectable disease or high-grade mucinous appendiceal carcinoma has no disease-specific systemic therapy; management focuses on preventing and managing bowel obstruction from mucin accumulation.
Palliative laparoscopic evacuation of mucinous ascites can relieve symptoms in unresectable disease; plain needle paracentesis is largely ineffective against the viscous mucin.

Pressurized intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy is an emerging option for unresectable peritoneal carcinomatosis broadly, extrapolated from colorectal and gastric peritoneal disease experience rather than specific to this condition.

For high-grade or truly unresectable disease, systemic fluoropyrimidine and platinum-based chemotherapy following general gastrointestinal mucinous adenocarcinoma approaches may be used, though low-grade disease responds poorly given its indolent biology.
Recurrence after initial cytoreductive surgery can still respond well to a repeat cytoreductive operation, so recurrence should be reassessed at a specialist center rather than assumed futile.
Surveillance uses cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI as needed) and serum tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, CA125) to track disease burden and detect recurrence over long-term follow-up.
Any suspected or confirmed case should be referred promptly to a specialist surgical oncology center experienced in cytoreductive surgery and perioperative intraperitoneal chemotherapy.

Diagnostic uncertainty about the primary site, such as appendiceal versus mucinous ovarian versus another gastrointestinal origin, should prompt pathology and gastrointestinal review before major surgery is planned.
